prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part for optical lattice clocks, credited to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. After reading all eight first-round statements, the case rests on three points that survived every objection raised. First, the concept is original and specific: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the conflict between holding many neutral atoms tightly and leaving the clock transition unperturbed. That is a statement about atomic structure and light shifts, which I can judge directly as an atomic theorist. Second, the realisation changed what can be measured. A large ensemble of Fermi-degenerate atoms, with trap shifts cancelled, gives accuracy and stability together, which neither a single trapped ion nor a comb-referenced microwave standard offered. Ye's group took this to the 10^-18 level, resolved millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and treated many-body interactions in the lattice as something to control. Third, the result has been reproduced and surpassed in several laboratories over about two decades, so recognition is neither premature nor dependent on an unsettled interpretation. I treat the seven-of-eight convergence as a prompt to test the arguments, not as evidence in itself; the arguments of originality, confirmation and a clean two-name credit hold up when I test them against the alternatives. On the chair's questions: I regard the redefinition of the second as supporting evidence only, not a condition. The scientific achievement is complete without it, and making the prize wait on a metrological decision outside physics would put the committee's timing in other hands. My citation wording now names the magic-wavelength lattice and both accuracy and stability, to state in the text what separates this from the 2005 and 2012 citations.
statement.case_against: The reservation I weigh most is still distinctness from the 2005 prize for the comb and precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize for control of single trapped ions. A colleague who weighs discovery in nature above capability could fairly say this is the next step in a line already honoured, and Danielsson says so explicitly. My answer is that the citation can and should name the lattice concept and the combination of accuracy and stability, which the earlier prizes did not. But I accept that this is a judgement, and I would not claim it is proven. The second reservation is attribution: Takamoto and colleagues in Katori's group made the first strontium lattice clock measurements, and PTB, NIST, SYRTE, RIKEN and the ion-clock groups contributed to the same race. A three-person limit cannot accommodate all of them, and I cannot verify the priority record from the supplied material. I do not think adding a third name would improve fairness unless there is a specific, documented claim, and none is in the record. The third is that the prize honours an instrument and a measurement capability, which is a narrower kind of discovery than a new phenomenon.

responses.point: Argues that the adjacent prizes support rather than undermine the clocks, asks whether the citation should address Takamoto and other Sr-lattice colleagues, and ranks B016 below B023; his stay in Hall's laboratory at JILA is a disclosure item.
responses.response: I agree that the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured what made the lattice clock possible, and that supports distinctness, but I would not call the question closed, since Danielsson and Johansson are not answered by the sentence alone. The citation has to carry the argument. On Takamoto, I do not think the citation wording can or should list Sr-lattice colleagues. A phrase like 'invention and realisation' already separates the concept from the later development, and the supplied record does not contain a claim that would justify replacing either credited name. On his disclosure, a doctoral stay in the laboratory of John Hall, with no tie to Katori or Ye, is a historical relationship to a different person and does not seem to me to require more than the disclosure he has made. I accept his ordering of B023 over B016, and I now list B023 instead of B016 as my second alternative for the reason he gives: B016 is mainly an enabling technique with the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram still open.

responses.point: Weighs a clue found in nature most heavily, concedes B004 is the cleaner two-name case, and says B032 may be the stronger case in a year or two if the source picture sharpens.
responses.response: I take the point that a prize for an instrument is a different kind of recognition from one for a new window on the universe, and I do not claim that clocks are the more consequential discovery. Where I differ is on whether the committee can act on B032 this year. The diffuse flux is established, but the sources are not, and his own statement says the roles of Halzen, Karle and Yoshida rest on recollection and that a three-name IceCube prize would be contested. A prize in a year in which the allocation cannot be defended is a worse outcome than a prize in a year in which it can, and the same standard would apply to a later B032 prize. On the question he put to the committee, whether we are choosing the comfortable attribution over the consequential discovery, I think that is a fair worry for the committee to carry forward, but here the choice is between a settled discovery with a clean credit and an important one with an open credit. I would not want to make that trade against the physics, and I do not think I am doing so.

responses.point: Prefers B010 as a single part but accepts that the attribution and maturity case for B004 is the strongest on the table and that B004 is his first alternative; asks whether an open pairing mechanism should delay recognition.
responses.response: I appreciate his concession on B004 and I accept the distinction he draws: the discovery honoured in B010 is the existence of correlated insulating and superconducting states at the magic angle, which is reproduced by several groups, and not the pairing glue. That is a fair historical point, since precedent does not require a mechanism before recognition. My remaining hesitation is narrower. It concerns the allocation, not the maturity argument alone. Cao's first authorship, the Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto continuum-model work and the parallel groups mean the three-name limit leaves out credits that people in the field will name, and Olsson's two-name variant and his three-name version disagree on Bistritzer. I think B010 is the strongest candidate for a later year, and I keep it as my first alternative. If Eriksson and others bring a documented account of the early experimental history to round two, I would reconsider the order of B010 and B004 in the vote on that basis.

responses.point: Set aside her first-ranked B010 for maturity and credit, concedes the experimental credit problem, and would keep B010 as an alternative for a later year.
responses.response: I value her saying plainly that the physics of B010 was not the reason she moved. That separates the question of scientific quality from the question of readiness, which is how I read it as well, and it means B010 is held back by credit and timing, not by doubt. I agree with her view that the 2018 experimental credit is the harder problem than the pairing mechanism. Where I would add to it is that this is a reason for the committee to record, in its own notes, what it would need to see: a documented account of the early experimental history and a settled view on whether Bistritzer is part of the prediction credit. Her pair, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and Eriksson's trio cannot both be right, and that disagreement is itself a sign the allocation is not yet ready.

responses.point: Moved B004 from eighth to a preferred position, says Ye is credited under other candidate lines, and does not want to pair B023 with another atoms-and-lattices part because of the Cirac and Zoller overlap.
responses.response: I agree with his reasoning on partition: the overlap between B016 and B023 means a two-part prize combining either of them with B004 would force either a name outside the three-person limit or a split I cannot defend scientifically, so I stay with a single part. On his statement that Ye is credited under other candidate lines, the shortlist file shows Ye only under B004, and I see no other shortlisted ballot that names him. I read that sentence as an error in the first-round text, and I would ask him to confirm. If Ye were in another ballot it would matter for balance, but as it stands it does not weigh on my configuration. I also welcome his candour about moving from eighth to a preferred position, and I note that his stated reasons were the scientific arguments of his colleagues and not the support count.

responses.point: Argues the overlap worry is better answered by keeping the lattice-clock prize single, and says he relies on unverified recollection about early Sr lattice priority.
responses.response: I agree that a single part is the better configuration, for the same partition reason. I share his caution about priority: I too cannot verify the early Sr lattice record from the supplied text, and I would want that stated in the committee record rather than treated as settled. Where I would go slightly further is that his unverified recollection and my own uncertainty point in the same direction. Neither of us has found a documented claim that displaces Katori or Ye, and in the absence of such a claim the proposal and realisation split is the defensible reading. If a documented priority claim appears before the vote, it should change the names and not only the wording of the citation.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues accept the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I judge it distinct but not provably so, and the citation wording is where that judgement is expressed.

Whether the early Sr-lattice work by Takamoto and others in Katori's group, or work at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN, gives a documented claim that should alter the names; I cannot verify this from the supplied record.
How the committee weighs an instrument and measurement capability against a new phenomenon in nature if the committee is split on that criterion.
Whether B010 would be ready after one or two more years, given the unsettled early-experimental credit and the three-name limit.
I rely on my own background in atomic theory for the physics of the magic-wavelength condition and have not checked the experimental priority record beyond the supplied text.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict applies to B004: my profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye. My listed connections (Anne L'Huillier, the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group, Dahlström, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) match no credited name on the shortlist. I remain an atomic physicist working close to B004, B016 and B023, and I disclose that proximity of field. Kroll's disclosure of a past stay in Hall's laboratory at JILA does not, in my view, bear on B004 beyond being noted in the record.
